Mahean
Magamemnon

Hi, I’m Mahean. I recently founded Foresight Machines.

I originally hail from the Global South and grew up on a farm there. I got a proper internet connection for the first time on December 2, 2020.

I study computational sciences at Minerva University, which is backed by Benchmark, and live in a different country each semester. When I’m not abroad, I live in the great city of San Francisco.

Before that, I spent a year on the core investment team at M13, focused on AI and energy startups and building software for automation.

Some of my primal instincts are engineering foresight, engineering light in all its forms, and wondering at how much of space is still out there for us.

mahean888@gmail.comX / maheanmm

Interests

  • Simulation

    I got into it through the simulation hypothesis, mostly via Rizwan Virk’s book The Simulation Hypothesis, which connects it to science, religion and Eastern mysticism.

    These days I mostly think about simulating whole populations and the systems they live in, from a single company to a city to an entire economy. Foresight Machines is my attempt at it. I think it has only just become possible.

  • Superforecasting

    I’ve competed in forecasting tournaments and hosted them.

    This summer, AI forecasters matched the best human superforecasters for the first time. With more compute, better data and architectures built for the job, they’ll keep improving. A simulation is only as good as the forecasts you feed it.

  • Augmented reality

    My first software project, Oasis Labs, tried to build a spatial layer on top of physical reality. The bet was that the platform after the smartphone would be the world itself, with its own social life and commerce.

    Later I studied metamaterials, because glasses you wear every day need much thinner lenses. The closest thing I’ve seen to what I was trying to build is the Big Market in Valerian and the City of a Thousand Planets: a whole bazaar you can only see with a headset, sitting on top of an empty desert. I’m very optimistic.

  • Capital

    Which ideas get funded decides which futures get built.

    A year deploying venture capital at M13 left me thinking the biggest problems are time and speed: too little money for things that take a decade to prove, and too much process for small bets.

  • Bioluminescence

    Life spent billions of years in water before it reached land. That may be why most deep-sea animals make their own light and almost nothing on land does.

    I’d like to engineer it on land and make our pale blue dot a little more like Pandora. Laurelin.bio is my attempt to design that light de novo.

  • Space sustainability

    Launch costs have collapsed and orbit is filling up fast. A real economy is forming above us, and so is a debris problem.

    One of my first research projects, in my last year of school, used machine learning to map and track debris in low Earth orbit. It won the NASA Space Apps Challenge, and I’m still proud of it.

  • Strategy games

    I’ve spent thousands of hours on The Battle of Polytopia, been ranked in the global top 10 several times, and still play in its Diamond league.

    Wanting more depth, I built my own version of Azad, the game in Iain M. Banks’s The Player of Games. It’s roughly what I wish Polytopia would become.

  • Planetary engineering

    Rain where it’s needed, carbon pulled out of the air and turned to stone, and other ways of steering the climate deliberately. Rainmaker is a good example.

    I like thinking about which futures Earth could still have.

  • Aesthetics

    People take care of the places and things they find beautiful.

    I’m most drawn to solarpunk: architecture where technology and living things grow together. Laurelin.bio is partly my way of contributing to it.
